content.overview: BSA s. 23, Confession to police officer, is an evidentiary provision in the Relevancy of facts cluster. Analyse it through the separate questions of relevancy, admissibility, proof, burden and probative weight, and check BSA s. 170 for proceedings governed by the repeal and savings rule. Historical concordance: Indian Evidence Act s. 25.

content.study:
Current-law identity
BSA s. 23 governs confession to police officer within Chapter II - Relevancy of facts. The provision must be read with its enacted clauses, explanations, illustrations and connected provisions BSA s. 22, BSA s. 24. Historical concordance: Indian Evidence Act s. 25.

The forensic distinction
Relevancy asks whether a fact has the statutory connection required by the Adhiniyam. Admissibility asks whether the Court may receive that relevant material under the rules of exclusion, privilege, form and foundation. Proof asks whether the admitted material establishes the fact to the required standard. Probative weight asks how much reliance the Court should place on it. A relevant fact is not automatically admissible, and admissibility is not proof of the ultimate fact.

Mandatory application checklist
1. Identify the fact in issue, the fact sought to be introduced and the party tendering it.
2. State the exact rule in BSA s. 23, including every condition, explanation, proviso and illustration.
3. Classify the material as oral, documentary, electronic, real or circumstantial evidence.
4. Test directness, hearsay, privilege, primary or secondary evidence, authentication and statutory certificate requirements.
5. Identify the party bearing the initial burden under BSA s. 104 and any special-knowledge rule under s. 109.
6. Separate admissibility from the weight ultimately assigned after cross-examination and the complete record.

Electronic records and constitutional limits
Electronic and digital records are documents under BSA. Where a computer output, email, messaging record, CCTV export, call record, server log or device image is tendered through the statutory route, check BSA s. 63 and its certificate requirements. The certificate is not a substitute for relevance, authenticity, chain of custody or proof of the fact asserted. Evidence must also respect Articles 20(3), 21 and 14 of the Constitution, privilege rules and fair-trial disclosure.

Courtroom method
In a written submission, identify the fact in issue, show the statutory relevancy link, answer the admissibility objection, establish the foundation, identify the burden and standard, and explain the probative consequence. Do not cite the historical Evidence Act number as the current rule after 1 July 2024 except as concordance. Do not convert a missing certificate, hearsay statement or weak foundation into an automatic finding on the merits without analysing the applicable statutory consequence.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective and Evidentiary Foundation
sections.body:
BSA s. 23 regulates confession to police officer within Relevancy of facts.
The statutory scheme seeks reliable adjudication by limiting proof to legally relevant and properly received material.
Read the provision with the constitutional values of fair trial, privilege, reliability and equality of arms.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Exceptions and Connected Rules
sections.body:
Deconstruct every clause of BSA s. 23; do not replace the enacted rule with a one-line Evidence Act summary.
Read it with BSA s. 22, BSA s. 24. Connected provisions may control foundation, exclusion, presumptions, witnesses or the mode of proof.
Historical concordance assists comparison only and is not the current citation.

sections.heading: Mandatory Relevancy, Admissibility and Proof Ingredients
sections.body:
First ingredient: identify the fact in issue or the statutory relevancy link.
Second ingredient: satisfy any exclusion, privilege, directness, primary-document or foundation rule.
Third ingredient: prove authenticity and the source or maker where the form of evidence requires it.
Fourth ingredient: apply the correct burden and standard, then distinguish admissibility from probative weight.

sections.heading: BSA Burdens, Presumptions and Electronic Records
sections.body:
BSA s. 104 supplies the ordinary burden framework; the party asserting the legal proposition must establish its foundation.
BSA s. 109 addresses facts especially within knowledge. It does not erase the initial burden or permit conviction on an unproved charge.
For electronic records, examine BSA s. 63 certificate, device or system identity, production method, integrity, custody and the distinction between admissibility and weight.

sections.heading: Trial Roadmap, Forum, Limitation and Repeal Savings
sections.body:
Apply BSA s. 23 at the correct stage of trial or inquiry and identify whether the objection concerns tender, marking, admissibility, proof or final weight.
For proceedings governed by the post-1 July 2024 evidence regime, cite BSA. For proceedings saved by s. 170, identify the applicable Indian Evidence Act route before arguing the consequence.
Check the governing procedural statute and any special limitation rule for the application or appeal; evidence law itself does not create a universal limitation period.

examples.title: Example 1 - Foundation and admissibility satisfied
examples.body: A party identifies the fact in issue, establishes the statutory relevancy link under s. 23, proves the source and authenticity of the record, and satisfies the applicable documentary or electronic foundation. The Court may receive the material and then assess its weight.

examples.title: Example 2 - Relevancy does not cure a defect
examples.body: A party offers a relevant screenshot or hearsay statement but cannot satisfy the applicable statutory foundation, certificate, directness or privilege rule. The Court must analyse admissibility separately instead of treating logical relevance as automatic proof.

hypotheticals.question: Whether the material is relevant and admissible under BSA s. 23, and what proof and burden consequences follow.
hypotheticals.analysis: 1. Identify the fact in issue and the statutory relevancy route. 2. Test the form of evidence: direct oral evidence, documentary evidence, electronic record, hearsay or privileged communication. 3. Check the applicable foundation and BSA s. 63 certificate where digital material is tendered. 4. Place the initial burden under s. 104 and use s. 109 only after the foundation for special knowledge is established. 5. Separate admissibility from credibility and final probative weight.

misconceptions.trap: Citing only the old Evidence Act number for s. 23.
misconceptions.correction: Use BSA s. 23 for the current regime and mention the historical number only as concordance or when applying the s. 170 savings rule.

misconceptions.trap: Relevancy automatically means admissibility and proof.
misconceptions.correction: Relevancy, admissibility, proof and probative weight are separate forensic inquiries.

misconceptions.trap: BSA s. 109 reverses the entire burden of proof.
misconceptions.correction: The initial burden remains with the party asserting the legal proposition; special knowledge operates only on the facts within that statutory rule.

cases.name: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
cases.facts: The case concerned the proof and certification of electronic records tendered in election litigation.
cases.issue: Whether the statutory certificate requirement for computer outputs is mandatory and when secondary electronic evidence may be received.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The certificate requirement is a condition precedent for admissibility of the relevant electronic record output, subject to the statutory route and the Court's power to facilitate production where the facts justify it.
cases.holding: The Constitution Bench clarified the certificate rule and overruled the contrary view to the extent necessary.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 23 concerns electronic records or digital proof; it does not decide the relevancy or admissibility of every non-digital item.

cases.name: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
cases.facts: The Court examined the mode of proving electronic records in an election dispute.
cases.issue: Whether electronic records could be admitted without compliance with the statutory certificate route.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Electronic evidence must be proved through the special statutory requirements applicable to computer outputs; ordinary secondary-evidence principles cannot bypass that route.
cases.holding: The earlier contrary approach was displaced and the certificate discipline was reaffirmed.
cases.relevance: Use only for digital evidence issues connected with s. 23; distinguish it from ordinary oral, physical-document or privilege questions.

cases.name: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra
cases.facts: The Court assessed a prosecution based substantially on circumstantial evidence.
cases.issue: What standard must circumstantial evidence meet before it can support a criminal conviction.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The circumstances must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive in tendency, and form a complete chain excluding every reasonable hypothesis of innocence.
cases.holding: The Court restated the safeguards for conviction on circumstantial evidence.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 23 concerns circumstantial proof or inference; do not use it as a substitute for a section-specific relevancy rule.

learningObjectives: Master the statutory prohibition under Section 23(1) BSA: no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence.
Analyze the landmark statutory discovery exception under Section 23(2) BSA (re-enacting Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872).
Understand the precise legal limits of the discovery exception: only so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered is admissible.
Evaluate the constitutional interface between Section 23(2) discovery recoveries and Article 20(3) protection against self-incrimination.
enhancement.definition: BSA s. 23 governs confessions made to police officers and the discovery exception. Under sub-section (1), no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence. Under sub-section (2), provided that when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of such information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly thereby to the fact thereby discovered, may be proved.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Protection against custodial coercion and the guarantee of physical objective corroboration. Confessions made to police are excluded due to inherent danger of torture and fabrication; the discovery exception admits only that narrow fragment of information whose truth is objectively verified by the physical recovery of tangible evidence.
statutoryFramework: Chapter II — Relevancy of Facts, BSA s. 23.
Sub-section (1): Absolute exclusionary rule — ban on proving confessions made to any police officer.
Sub-section (2): Statutory discovery exception — information leading to discovery of physical facts in police custody.
The "Distinctly" Relates Test: Strict evidentiary filter admitting only the information directly responsible for locating the hidden object.
Constitutional Anchor: Tested and upheld under Article 20(3) of the Constitution (privilege against compelled self-incrimination).
essentialIngredients: General Exclusion (s. 23(1)): A statement made to a police officer amounting to an admission of guilt is completely inadmissible.
(a) Information given by a person accused of an offence;
(b) The accused was in the custody of a police officer at the time of giving the information;
(c) A physical fact is discovered in consequence of that information;
(d) The fact was previously hidden and unknown to the police; and
(e) Only so much of the statement as relates distinctly to the discovered fact is admissible.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 23 BSA is one of the most litigated provisions in Indian criminal trials, consolidating Sections 25, 26, and 27 of the repealed Indian Evidence Act, 1872 into a single unified statutory provision.

Under Section 23(1), Indian law enacts an **uncompromising exclusionary rule**: no confession made to a police officer, of any rank, can be proved against an accused. Unlike English or American law (where voluntary police confessions are admissible if Miranda warnings are administered), Indian law presumes that custodial statements to police are tainted by coercion, fear, or inducement. Even if a confession is written and signed in the police station, it is inadmissible.

However, Section 23(2) enacts the **Doctrine of Confirmation by Subsequent Facts** (the classic *Pulukuri Kottaya v. King-Emperor* rule). If the accused in police custody gives information that leads the police directly to the recovery of a hidden physical article (such as a murder weapon, stolen gold, or dead body) from a place of concealment unknown to the police, the information is partially admitted.

Crucially, Section 23(2) admits **only that portion of the statement which relates distinctly to the discovery**. The confession of guilt itself remains excluded. For example, if an accused states: *"I killed the deceased with a dagger, and I have buried that dagger under the banyan tree behind the old mill"*, the court will redact the statement. The words *"I killed the deceased with a dagger"* are strictly excluded; only the words *"I have buried the dagger under the banyan tree"* are admissible under Section 23(2).
examples: Teaching illustration (Admissible Discovery under Section 23(2)): Accused A, while in police custody, states: "I have hidden the bloodstained knife used in the crime inside a hollow brick in the abandoned well." A then leads the police team and independent witnesses to the well, points to the brick, and retrieves the knife. The knife is tested and matches the victim’s blood. The statement regarding where the knife was hidden and the recovery memo are admissible under Section 23(2) BSA.

Teaching illustration (Inadmissible Confessional Portion): Accused B states to the police: "I poisoned my business partner because he cheated me, and I threw the empty poison vial in the river." Divers search the river for three days but find nothing. The statement is completely inadmissible: without the actual discovery of a physical fact, Section 23(2) does not apply, and Section 23(1) bars the entire confession.
distinctions: BSA s. 23(1) vs BSA s. 23(2): Sub-section (1) is the general exclusionary rule barring police confessions; Sub-section (2) is a narrow proviso admitting only the specific information leading to the physical recovery.
Discovery of Fact vs Discovery of Object: The "fact discovered" includes not merely the physical object, but the place from which it is produced and the accused’s knowledge of that concealment.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether the statement of an accused in police custody: "I murdered X and hidden his gold wristwatch in my attic", followed by the recovery of the watch, can be admitted in its entirety.
Rule: Under Section 23(2) BSA, only so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact discovered is admissible; the confessional admission of guilt ("I murdered X") is inadmissible.
Application: The statement contains two parts: (1) confession of murder, and (2) location of the watch. Only the second part relates distinctly to the discovery.
Conclusion: The trial court must admit only the statement regarding the concealment and recovery of the watch; the admission of having murdered X must be redacted.

keyTakeaways: Section 23(1) BSA enacts an absolute prohibition on proving confessions made to police officers.
Section 23(2) permits proving information that leads directly to the discovery of a physical fact.
Only that part of the information which relates distinctly to the discovery is admissible; the confession of guilt is excluded.
Must be corroborated by the actual recovery of the hidden physical object from an undisclosed place.
